infra: TreeDataGrid vendored as a git submodule under third_party/ built from MIT source, NOT the NuGet package, to avoid the Avalonia Pro license gate
siblingModules: src/FileManager.Core/IPC/Handlers/ — 17 parallel IIpcRequestHandler implementations (DryRunHandler, RunProfileHandler, SaveProfileHandler, GetSettingsHandler, ...), the clearest parallel-implementation set in the repo
src/FileManager.UI/ViewModels/Settings/ — parallel setting-row/category view models (SettingItems, SettingsRows, SettingsCategoryViewModel, SettingsNavNodeViewModel, DriveOverridesSettingViewModel)
src/FileManager.Platform.Windows/ — flat set of Windows*Service/Provider adapters implementing Core/Platform/ abstractions
notes: No Directory.Build.props — every csproj repeats its own TargetFramework/Nullable/AOT settings.

Strict layering rule documented in src/FileManager.UI/FileManager.UI.csproj: the UI references Contracts ONLY; FileManager.Service is referenced with ReferenceOutputAssembly=false purely for build order + output copy (ServiceLauncher probes for FileManager.Service.exe beside the UI exe).

Two custom MSBuild targets in FileManager.UI.csproj are load-bearing: EnsureTreeDataGridSubmodule (fail-fast on missing submodule) and CopyServiceHostOutput (lays out the service beside the UI for F5).

FileManager.Core and FileManager.Platform.Windows are IsTrimmable + IsAotCompatible; Service and UI are PublishAot — reflection-based patterns are a real constraint and JSON must go through the source-gen context.
InvariantGlobalization=false on the Service is deliberate (timezone validation needs ICU).

docs/specs/architecture-v1.md is a detailed NORMATIVE design document (layering rules §1, project map §2, service catalog §4, DTO catalog §5, threading model §8, persistence layout §9, extension seams §10) and docs/specs/spec-draft-v3.md is the authoritative behavior spec — judge drift against these documents rather than against generic C# taste, and cite the section anchor when you do.
Repo is mid-feature on branch feature/live-single-job-vertical; the third_party/TreeDataGrid submodule is dirty in the working tree, and dry-run-pooling-plan.md sits untracked at the repo root.
Vendored third_party/ is excluded from the inventory and must NOT be reviewed or recommended for change.

frozenTypes.type: FileManager.Contracts.Profiles.Profile (and its entire graph: TriggerSettings, ScheduleSettings, SourceConfig, TransformerStep, TargetConfig, PolicySettings, FilterSet, AttributeFilterSettings, LoggingSettings)
frozenTypes.reason: Persisted as profiles/*.json on user machines and re-read on every service start. Property NAMES are the JSON keys; the record is round-tripped through System.Text.Json source-gen. Any profile written by an older build must still load, so EVERY type reachable from Profile is frozen: no renaming members, no splitting/merging records, no moving a member to a nested type. Profile.Id is additionally aliased to the wire name "ProfileId" and the file NAME is the Guid.

frozenTypes.type: All Profile enums: SyncMode, TargetLayout, ConflictResolution, OverwriteHandling, VerificationMethod, OnSuccessAction, OnFailureAction, MetadataOnConflict, ArgumentMode, OutputMode, MissedRunPolicy, LogVerbosity
frozenTypes.reason: Serialized BY NAME into profiles/*.json and over IPC (UseStringEnumConverter). Renaming a member silently invalidates every stored profile. VerificationMethod additionally pins wire names via [JsonStringEnumMemberName("XXH3-128"/"SHA256")] AND its declaration ORDER is a wire contract because journal records serialize enums as integers.

frozenTypes.type: FileManager.Contracts.IPC.IpcRequest and all 18 derived records (GetStatusRequest … ShutdownRequest)
frozenTypes.reason: Polymorphic wire format with a "type" discriminator table. The discriminator strings are duplicated in three places that must agree: the [JsonDerivedType] attributes, IpcRequestTypes' const table + DiscriminatorOf switch, and each handler's RequestType property used as the DI dispatch-table key. Deleting/renaming a derived record or changing a discriminator breaks UI↔service compatibility at runtime (NOT_IMPLEMENTED / IPC_MALFORMED), not at compile time.

frozenTypes.type: FileManager.Contracts.IPC.IpcResponse and all 16 derived records (OkResponse … RelocateProfilesResponse)
frozenTypes.reason: Same polymorphic "type" discriminator contract on the response side. IpcSerializer deliberately serializes through the BASE JsonTypeInfo — serializing as the derived type drops the discriminator and silently breaks the wire. Frame ORDER in the dry-run stream (chunks → progress → complete) is also contractual.

frozenTypes.type: FileManager.Contracts.IPC.EngineEvent and derived (JobStartedEvent, JobProgressEvent, JobCompletedEvent, JobFailedEvent, PauseChangedEvent, ProfilesChangedEvent, RunQueuedEvent, EngineWarningEvent)
frozenTypes.reason: Broadcast wire format with "type" discriminators. JobPhase's MEMBER ORDER is behaviorally load-bearing: the progress publisher drops any sample whose phase went backwards, so reordering members changes runtime behavior.

frozenTypes.type: IpcRequest.CurrentProtocolVersion / IpcRequest.ProtocolVersion
frozenTypes.reason: Version 6 handshake. A mismatched service/UI pair must fail loud with IPC_VERSION_MISMATCH. Any change to the request/response/event shapes requires a documented version bump, not a silent edit — the UI and service ship as separate executables and can be at different versions on one machine.

frozenTypes.type: FileManager.Core.Journal.JournalRecord and all 12 derived records (JobOpenedRecord … JobClosedRecord)
frozenTypes.reason: Write-ahead journal on disk (journal-NNNNNN.ndjsonl) read back by crash recovery at every service start. Discriminators are the short strings "open"/"sealed"/"twb"/"tver"/"tstg"/"tplc"/"tunc"/"tskp"/"commit"/"rbbegin"/"trb"/"close" under property name "t". A journal written before a crash MUST still replay — renaming a record, a property, or a discriminator loses in-flight user data.

frozenTypes.type: FileManager.Core.Journal.RollbackAction, FileManager.Core.Jobs.JobOutcome, FileManager.Core.Jobs.SkipReason (and the PolicySnapshot enums)
frozenTypes.reason: JournalJsonContext has no UseStringEnumConverter, so these serialize as INTEGERS into the on-disk journal. Member DECLARATION ORDER is the wire contract — new members must be appended only; reordering or removing one makes an existing journal replay as a different action. Explicitly annotated as such in-source.

persistedFormats.format: profiles/*.json — one file per profile, file name is the Guid in "D" format; written atomically (random temp + fsync + rename)
persistedFormats.risk: The whole Profile graph is frozen. The directory is USER-RELOCATABLE (settings.ProfilesDirectory, resolved live on every read), so any code that caches or hard-codes the profile directory breaks relocation. A load failure is a silent skip with a log warning — a schema break shows up as profiles quietly disappearing from the list, not as an error.

persistedFormats.format: settings.json (single file at the engine root, SchemaVersion 4) — written by the service, read INDEPENDENTLY by the UI at startup for the theme
persistedFormats.risk: Two readers, one writer, across two processes and two assemblies. A corrupt/unloadable file falls back to defaults SILENTLY — a property rename does not error, it resets the user's settings. The v1→v2 migration shim (raw JsonDocument) must survive.

persistedFormats.format: journal/journal-NNNNNN.ndjsonl — append-only, fsync'd write-ahead log, 'J1 <crc32:x8> <json>\n' per line, rotated by size
persistedFormats.risk: HIGHEST data-loss risk in the repo. Crash recovery MUST replay journals written by the previous build before the IPC server starts (I-RECOVER-FIRST). Enums serialize as INTEGERS here. Any change to a record type, discriminator, property, enum ordering, or the frame prefix makes in-flight jobs unrecoverable and can strand or destroy staged user files.

persistedFormats.format: audit/audit-YYYYMM.ndjsonl — deletion audit trail, monthly files, NEVER auto-deleted, same J1 framing
persistedFormats.risk: Unbounded retention means records of arbitrary age must still parse. The reader only reads the 1 MiB tail and skips malformed lines with a warning, so a format break degrades to silently empty audit history.
A shape change resets the global pause flag; the engine would resume processing on a machine the user had paused.

persistedFormats.format: <scratch>/*.snapshot — dry-run spool spill files, hand-written/hand-read trimmed JSON
persistedFormats.risk: Same-machine, same-version by design (each run deletes its own; startup purges leftovers), so the format is comparatively free — BUT the writer and reader are two halves of one hand-maintained format with omitted-field reconstruction (source op path/root, subject-targeting dest op path). Change one half only and records deserialize with the WRONG PATHS rather than failing.

persistedFormats.format: logs/jobs/<jobId:N>.log and rolling logs/service-YYYYMMDD.log, logs/ui-YYYYMMDD.log (14-day retention)
persistedFormats.risk: Job logs are fetched over IPC by job id; the file name derivation is the lookup key. The UI's log-folder action and the service's writer must agree on the directory.
Read/write failures are swallowed and fall back to defaults; a schema break silently resets layout. Deliberately NOT part of GlobalSettings — do not merge it in.

persistedFormats.format: Exported profile .json (single profile, on-disk format, written atomically, never overwriting)
persistedFormats.risk: An INTERCHANGE format: exported files must round-trip back through Import, including files exported by older builds and files shared between machines. Uses the same FileManagerJsonContext.Profile as the profile store, so it inherits the whole frozen graph.

persistedFormats.format: IPC wire: 4-byte LE length prefix + UTF-8 JSON, 16 MiB frame cap, over named pipe filemanager-<user>; ProtocolVersion 6 handshake
persistedFormats.risk: UI and service are separate executables that can be at different versions on one machine, and the service may already be RUNNING (started at logon) when a new UI connects. Any message-shape change requires a protocol version bump; without one, the pair half-parses instead of failing loud.

persistedFormats.format: On-disk infrastructure markers inside USER target roots: <root>/.fm_staging/<jobId:N>/<index>-<name>, <tempRoot>/.pipeline_tmp/<jobId>/, <finalName>.fmtmp-<hex>
persistedFormats.risk: These sit inside the user's own folders. Crash recovery finds staged PRIOR VERSIONS of overwritten user files by this exact path shape; scans exclude them by name. Change either and recovery cannot restore what it staged, or the tool's own temp files start being treated as user content to copy.
Live OS state on the user's machine; both register and unregister key off the literal value name. Also assumes a self-contained deployment where ProcessPath IS the service exe.

constraints.notes:
SCOPE NOTE: `git ls-files` outside src/tests/benchmarks was searched too. Nothing in the repo does assembly scanning, `Activator.CreateInstance`, `Type.GetType`, or attribute-driven discovery of application types — the architecture spec FORBIDS them (AOT constraint) and every dispatch is an explicit table. The only reflection in shipping code is `EnumTitleExtensions.GetTitle` reading `[Tooltip]` off enum FIELD NAMES (src/FileManager.UI/Extensions/EnumTitleExtensions.cs:16), and reflection in tests that pins contracts (tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/IpcRequestTypesTests.cs:17 enumerates `[JsonDerivedType]`). So the compiler-invisible coupling here is NOT reflection — it is (a) persisted formats, (b) XAML, (c) hand-maintained parallel tables.

THREE HAND-MAINTAINED PARALLEL TABLES. Each must be edited together; the compiler checks none of the cross-links:
1. IpcRequest `[JsonDerivedType]` ↔ IpcRequestTypes consts + DiscriminatorOf switch ↔ handler.RequestType ↔ Program.cs DI list. (Guarded, partially: IpcRequestTypesTests pins 1↔2. Nothing pins the DI list — a handler missing there just answers NOT_IMPLEMENTED.)
2. EnginePaths.Default() ↔ UiPaths ↔ GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory/DefaultScratchDirectory. Sanctioned duplication (§1 rule 3: UI may reference Contracts only). Do NOT propose consolidating these into a shared type — that would break the layering rule. Do flag them if one drifts.
3. IpcEndpoint.Resolve() (Contracts, client side) ↔ WindowsIpcEndpointProvider (Core/Platform, server side). Deliberately duplicated per §4.11.

LAYERING IS A HARD CONSTRAINT ON MOVES. References point strictly downward: Contracts (BCL only) ← Core ← Platform.Windows ← hosts. Core must contain zero OS-specific code (the single sanctioned `OperatingSystem.IsWindows()` probe is NormalizedPath's case-sensitivity at src/FileManager.Core/Jobs/Job.cs:38). UI and any future CLI reference Contracts ONLY — never Core. So "move this shared helper to Core" is illegal for anything the UI uses, and "move this type to Contracts" is only legal if it needs nothing outside the BCL.

AOT/TRIM IS A CONSTRAINT ON TECHNIQUE. Core, Contracts and Platform.Windows are IsAotCompatible/IsTrimmable; both exes PublishAot. Any refactor that introduces reflection-based serialization, `Activator.CreateInstance`, runtime proxies, classic COM interop attributes, or config-binding frameworks compiles fine and fails only in a published build. Every serializable type must be listed in a JsonSerializerContext.

COMPILED BINDINGS COVER MOST XAML — BUT NOT ALL. `AvaloniaUseCompiledBindingsByDefault=true` means most binding-path typos are build errors. The exceptions are four `x:CompileBindings="False"` regions in DryRunView.axaml (lines 62, 111, 506, 644) plus every DataTemplate `DataType=` type key in SettingsWindow.axaml and every resource-key string emitted from view models — all resolved at RUNTIME. Treat DryRunTreeNode / DryRunFileRow / DryRunDestinationRow command names, the setting-editor view-model type names, and the Icon*/Brush.* key strings as a public API.

ORDER-AS-CONTRACT (three places where reordering members changes behavior, not just names): JobPhase declaration order (progress publisher drops backwards samples); VerificationMethod / RollbackAction / JobOutcome / SkipReason ordinals (journal writes enums as ints); DryRunReport's four list orders (ops reference files by integer index, and the streaming client appends chunks in receive order).

WHAT LOOKS LIKE DEAD CODE BUT IS NOT: `DryRunSnapshotJsonContext` (src/FileManager.Core/DryRun/DryRunSnapshotJsonContext.cs:10) is unused by production — it is retained ON PURPOSE as the naïve full-record baseline that the read-back benchmark measures the trimmed hand-written format against. `SettingsService.MigrateLegacy` is a back-compat shim for pre-v2 settings.json. Profile members marked `[reserved — fails v1 validation]` (SyncMode.Mirror, VerificationMethod.SizeTimestamp, ArgumentMode.Shell, FilterSet.ContentHashDedupe) are deliberate extension points, not unimplemented cruft — Mirror in particular IS live in the dry-run path.

THE 17 IPC HANDLERS ARE NOT A DUPLICATION CANDIDATE. They are the intentional replacement for reflection-based handler discovery (§4.9, AOT). Their shape similarity is the point.

GUARD TESTS THAT WILL CATCH SOME BREAKS (worth running after any change to the frozen surface): tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/IpcRequestTypesTests.cs (dispatch table vs. wire discriminators), tests/FileManager.Contracts.Tests/IPC/SerializationTests.cs, tests/FileManager.UI.Tests/ResourceKeyContractTests.cs (every icon/brush key a view model can emit resolves in the real App.axaml), and the *SmokeTests in tests/FileManager.UI.Tests (headless XAML load per window).

NOT PUBLIC API: nothing here is consumed as a library outside the repo — there are no NuGet packages produced and no public SDK. The external surface is instead operational: the FileManager.Service.exe file name, the named pipe, the HKCU Run value, the two env-var overrides (FILEMANAGER_SERVICE_EXE, FILEMANAGER_PIPE_NAME), and the on-disk layout under %LOCALAPPDATA%\FileManager.

synthesis.executiveSummary:
This is a well-architected codebase with a disciplined core — strict downward layering, explicit AOT-safe dispatch tables, atomic writes with an fsync'd write-ahead journal, and a frozen-format register that the code visibly respects. The problems are not architectural drift; they are three narrower structural weaknesses that the design's own strengths have made easy to miss.

The most expensive one is that failures are routinely converted into successes at the boundary between a subsystem and the user. The pattern repeats independently in six places: a post-commit source disposition that fails (locked file, full archive, a rejected Recycle Bin call) is written to the journal and the job log and then returned as `JobOutcome.Succeeded` with a null Error, so the activity row is green and the status bar's LastError is cleared; a deletion whose audit-append fails destroys the file and loses the only record of it, and still reports success; directories the scanner cannot open are downgraded from Fatal to Warning and then logged and discarded by both the dry-run engine and the manual-run handler, so the user approves a `PermanentDelete` run against a plan that silently covered a partial tree; a failed catalog reload after a profile save or delete is logged at warning level and reported as OK, leaving the engine executing the stale profile — including a stale `OnSuccessAction`; a settings load that fails leaves the Settings dialog fully populated with constructor defaults, and the next Save persists those defaults over the real settings.json, resetting a relocated `ProfilesDirectory` and making the user's entire profile list vanish; and an unparseable settings.json is replaced by defaults with the original bytes left to be overwritten by that same next save. Individually each is a few lines. Collectively they mean the product's safety story — dry run first, then dispose of sources — has holes precisely at the points where the user is being asked to trust it. Every one of these is fixable without touching a frozen format: `EngineWarningEvent` already exists on the wire and is already routed to the UI's notice bar.

The second weakness is that the compiler-invisible coupling the repo depends on is only partly guarded. The register documents three hand-maintained parallel tables; `IpcRequestTypesTests` pins one leg of one of them. The unguarded leg has already drifted: the flagship end-to-end test hand-rebuilds the DI graph under a comment claiming parity with Program.cs and registers 14 handlers where production registers 17 — missing `DryRunStreamHandler`, which is the handler the UI uses for *every* dry run. Program.cs itself lists all 17 handler types twice by hand. In the UI, three row types share five command names that are bound by reflection inside `x:CompileBindings="False"` regions, held in step by nothing but a comment on each type. None of these produce a compile error when they break; they produce a NOT_IMPLEMENTED response or a dead right-click menu item.

The third is that one capability is implemented twice and the copies have already diverged in ways that matter. `AtomicPlacer` and `CrashRecovery` both implement the staged-overwrite `File.Replace` → two-step-move fallback; the placer's copy guards the fallback with `File.Exists(finalPath)` and documents that idempotency as mandatory, and the recovery copy — the one that replays the same journal rows on every service start — omits the guard, so a recovery pass interrupted between the two moves strands the final name absent forever. `DryRunEngine` carries a complete batched simulation pipeline alongside the streamed one that the UI actually uses, and the memory bound added to the streamed sweep was never applied to the batched half. `DryRunSourcesTab` and `DryRunDestinationsTab` are ~390 byte-identical lines of the same tab mechanism written twice, in the file that carries 42 of the repo's 128 commits — a memory-leak fix and a parallelization change were each demonstrably applied twice in a single diff.

The shape of the fix is: first close the silent-success holes and the dead code (small, reversible, each verified by one new test); then add the guards that convert runtime-silent coupling into compile errors or red tests; then, and only with characterization tests and benchmarks in place, consolidate the two genuinely duplicated implementations.

Scope honesty: this review covered `src/`, `tests/` and `benchmarks/` by reading and searching only — nothing was built, run, or profiled. `third_party/TreeDataGrid` and the PowerShell integration harnesses were treated as frozen and not assessed. Four areas could be assessed only by reading because they have no tests at all and, in three cases, cannot be constructed by a test: `EngineHost`'s startup ordering (the I-RECOVER-FIRST invariant), the service composition root, `IpcGateway`'s reconnect and poison-recycle rules, and `ScanScheduler`'s worker pool lifecycle. Confidence in those four is correspondingly lower, and the roadmap treats making them testable as work in its own right rather than assuming they are correct.

themes.theme: Failures silently reported as success at the user boundary
themes.description: The dominant cost in the repo. Six independent code paths convert a real failure into a clean success or a silent empty result: post-commit disposition failure returns JobOutcome.Succeeded with a null Error and clears LastError; a failed deletion-audit append still reports the delete as clean; enumeration faults are downgraded to warnings and then dropped by both dry-run and manual-run consumers, so the plan the user approves claims a complete tree; a failed catalog reload after save/delete reports OK while the engine keeps executing the stale profile; a failed settings load leaves the dialog on constructor defaults that the next Save writes over the user's real settings.json; an unparseable settings.json is replaced by defaults with no copy kept. The common root is that these subsystems have a logging channel but no result channel back to the caller, even though EngineWarningEvent already exists on the wire and is already routed to the UI notice bar. Two of these can lose user data outright (a relocated ProfilesDirectory reset; a PermanentDelete run approved against a partial plan).

themes.theme: Compiler-invisible coupling that nothing guards, and has already drifted
themes.description: The architecture deliberately trades reflection for hand-maintained tables (AOT constraint) and deliberately opts four XAML regions out of compiled bindings. Both are sound choices, but only one leg of one table is pinned by a test. The consequences are already visible: the end-to-end smoke test's hand-rebuilt DI graph is missing three handlers including the one the UI uses for every dry run; Program.cs lists all 17 handlers twice with nothing linking the lists; three dry-run row types share five reflection-bound command names held together by a comment; and the destination-kind key/icon/brush vocabulary is restated in seven places where a mismatch renders a blank glyph or a chip that filters nothing. Every failure in this theme is runtime-silent. The fix is uniformly cheap — a marker interface, DI enumeration of explicit registrations, one key-set assertion — and converts each into a build error or a red test.

themes.theme: One capability implemented twice, with the copies already diverged
themes.description: Three cases, ordered by damage. (1) The staged-overwrite replace primitive exists in AtomicPlacer and again in CrashRecovery; the placer's fallback is idempotent by explicit design and the recovery copy is not, which is a latent data-stranding bug on the single most safety-critical write in the product. (2) DryRunEngine maintains a complete batched pipeline beside the streamed one; only the streamed half has a production client, and the sweep memory bound added to it was never applied to the batched half. (3) DryRunSourcesTab and DryRunDestinationsTab are ~390 byte-identical lines of one tab mechanism, in the file carrying 33% of all commits — a leak fix and a parallelization change were each applied twice in one diff. The root is the same in all three: no shared abstraction was introduced when a second caller appeared, so hardening lands on whichever copy the author was looking at.

themes.theme: The service's startup and transport layers cannot be constructed by a test
themes.description: EngineHost is internal in an assembly with no InternalsVisibleTo, so the I-RECOVER-FIRST ordering — crash recovery must complete before the IPC server accepts connections, bridges must be installed after catalog.Reload() and before the orchestrator starts — is asserted nowhere, even though CrashRecovery itself has 1085 lines of tests. The DI graph lives inline in Program.Main and is likewise unbuildable, which is why the smoke test's hand-copy drifted. IpcGateway acquires connections through static ServiceLauncher/IpcClient calls over a sealed private-constructor type, so its poison-recycle and error-code drop rules — the entire service-restart recovery story — have no test file. ScanScheduler's process-wide OS-thread ceiling is a private int behind a 15-second private const. These are not defects; they are the reason a defect in any of them would be invisible, and they gate the structural work in Tier 3.

themes.theme: Static and default-valued seams that quietly defeat injection
themes.description: The engine has a clean injectable EnginePaths root, but the two directories that hold user data escape it: GlobalSettings.ProfilesDirectory and .ScratchDirectory fall back to process-global statics, and SettingsService returns those without rebasing on the injected paths — so the end-to-end test needs a hand-written pin (with a comment explaining why) for profiles, and has none at all for scratch, meaning a spilling dry run in the test suite writes into the developer's real %LOCALAPPDATA%. Similarly SourceScanner's IVolumeInfoProvider is an optional parameter whose null branch collapses every path to one synthetic volume, so the per-volume thread-budget routing that ScanScheduler exists to implement is a production-only code path that no test or benchmark exercises. RunProfileHandler's detached Task.Run with CancellationToken.None is the same shape: work with no owner and no observable lifetime.

themes.theme: Accreted dead code, concentrated in the hottest file
themes.description: Low cost individually, but notable for where it sits: ten computed properties on the dry-run row records with no binding and no caller (including HasDestructiveAction, one character from the real HasDestructiveActions, in a file with reflection-bound regions), a telemetry counter that is never incremented so both completion logs permanently report '0 existing-target stats', an unreferenced spool factory that is a second construction path for a persisted snapshot format, and two dotnet-new scaffolding tests. All four are compiler-verified or grep-verified deletions.

themes.theme: Shell view model absorbing workflow implementation
themes.description: Lowest-cost theme, included because it explains an asymmetry rather than a size problem. MainWindowViewModel legitimately owns cross-view-model routing, but the profile-import workflow does raw File.OpenRead + JsonSerializer.Deserialize inline while the symmetric export routes through a dedicated Services/ProfileExport helper whose own doc says exported files must round-trip back through Import. There is no ProfileImport counterpart, so the two halves of a documented interchange format have no single place to check, and the safety invariant that imports arrive Active = false is an inline `with` expression reachable only through a folder-picker fake.

roadmap.title: Stop the Settings dialog from overwriting real settings after a failed load
roadmap.rationale: Highest impact-to-effort item in the entire review and it is one bool in one file. SettingsViewModel.LoadAsync returns early at :433 and :465 leaving the constructor defaults from :88-92 in place; SaveAsync (:479) is gated only on IsBusy and rebuilds a complete GlobalSettings at :525-541. The service is a separate process that can be mid-restart for ordinary reasons, so this is reachable by a user simply opening Settings at the wrong moment and changing the theme. Because ProfileStore resolves ProfilesDirectory live from settings on every read, the result is the user's entire profile list disappearing. Do this before anything else touches SettingsViewModel.

Do NOT gate SaveCommand.CanExecute on the new flag — the 18 existing SaveCommand tests construct the VM without ever calling LoadAsync and must stay green.

SettingsService.Load returns GlobalSettings.Default from its catches at :97-107 and from the deserialized-to-null branch at :90, leaving the unreadable file in place for the next atomic Update to overwrite. Ten computed properties on the dry-run row records occur exactly once each in the repo — at their own declaration — including HasDestructiveAction (one character from the real HasDestructiveActions, a genuine hazard in a reflection-bound region) and IsSingle, whose doc comment falsely claims a template binds it. DestinationProjector.Sweep takes a maxEntries budget defaulting to int.MaxValue; DryRunStreamHandler.cs:178-181 passes a real one with a comment explaining why, and DryRunEngine.cs:204-206 omits it, materializing one PhysicalFile plus one VirtualFileOperation per pre-existing destination file before the byte budget trims anything. MaxBatchCandidates already exists as the batched cap. Not reachable from production today (no client sends DryRunRequest), which is why it is a Tier 1 hygiene item rather than a bug fix — do it because it costs nothing. EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE: do not retire DryRunHandler/DryRunRequest/DryRunResponse and do not bump the protocol version; that is a separate Tier 3 decision.

CronExpression is a 127-line hand-rolled 5-field parser with six distinct rejection branches; `git grep CronExpression` over tests/ returns nothing, and its whole exercise is two lines in ProfileValidatorTests, one of which fails on field count rather than any value rule. The class doc states the scheduler will reuse this exact type for next-occurrence evaluation, so the grammar is about to become load-bearing for two consumers while unpinned — and a grammar regression silently reclassifies a stored schedule as invalid, which blocks the profile from saving.

ResourceKeyContractTests.cs:16-28 enumerates only ActivityRow's keys; IconUntouched, IconAdd, IconTrash and Brush.Warning are emitted by DryRunViewModel and covered by nothing, so a typo in any of the seven restatement sites ships silently — adding them is a two-line theory-data edit that makes App.axaml the arbiter. roadmap.title: Consolidate the staged-overwrite replace primitive and fix the non-idempotent recovery copy
roadmap.rationale: The single most valuable behavior-preserving change in the review, and it fixes a real latent bug rather than tidying. AtomicPlacer.TwoStepReplace guards its fallback with `if (File.Exists(finalPath))` and its doc states the idempotency is mandatory because 'a retry after the first move succeeded but the second failed would throw FileNotFound forever and strand the final name absent'. CrashRecovery.Replace at :470-478 does the same two moves unguarded — and it is called from the replay path that re-runs the same journal rows on EVERY service start, which is precisely the re-run scenario the guard was written for. Extract src/FileManager.Core/Files/StagedReplace.cs with the idempotent body and call it from both sites. Do NOT fold in RollbackExecutor.TryReplace — it replaces in the opposite direction with a null backup and overwrite:true, a genuinely different operation. Keep CrashRecovery's recovery-specific LogError+rethrow catch-all in place around the call.

It fails before the change and passes after; that is the proof. tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Placement/AtomicPlacerTests.cs must stay green unchanged (the placer's behavior does not move).

roadmap.title: Surface post-commit disposition and audit-write failures instead of reporting Succeeded
roadmap.rationale: The most user-visible of the silent-success holes. OnSuccess disposition is a promise the run-confirmation dialog makes to the user by name; when it fails, JobExecutor.cs:225-228 records it only in the job-closed journal record and the per-job log, then :237 returns Succeeded with a null Error, and JobOrchestrator.cs:229 clears _lastError. Nothing ever reads DispositionError back. Add a `DispositionError` init property to JobCompletion, carry it through, and in PublishCompletion set _lastError and publish an EngineWarningEvent — an existing wire type already routed by MainWindowViewModel.HandleEngineEvent to the activity notice bar, so no protocol bump. Explicitly do NOT add a JobOutcome member: JobOutcome is int-serialized into the journal and stringified onto the wire.

roadmap.verification: Extend the existing disposition-failure test in tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/Jobs/JobExecutorDispositionTests.cs (which already asserts closed.DispositionError at :101) to also assert completion.DispositionError. Add a JobOrchestrator test using the existing FakeJobExecutor returning a Succeeded completion with DispositionError set, asserting an EngineWarningEvent was published and GetStatus().LastError is non-null. All JobExecutor* suites stay green — Outcome remains Succeeded. CAUTION on the audit half (SourceDispositionService.Record returning Result<..., JobError>): it must surface through the same warning channel and must NOT turn a successful copy+disposition into JobOutcome.Failed.

roadmap.title: Report directories the scan could not read, in both the manual run and the dry run
roadmap.rationale: The safety-critical half of the silent-success theme: SourceScanner.cs:119-125 downgrades a subdirectory's Fatal enumeration fault to a Warning so siblings continue (correct), and then every consumer logs and discards it — DryRunEngine.cs:494 and RunProfileHandler.cs:113, with RunQueuedEvent.Error set only for a Fatal. ACL-denied, locked and offline-placeholder directories are routine on Windows, so the user reads a complete-looking plan with a full file count and space projection, then approves a run whose OnSuccess may be MoveToTrash or PermanentDelete. The repo's own stance is that partiality must be surfaced — DryRunViewModel.TruncationNotice spells out a truncated report in detail. Ship the manual-run half first: it is self-contained (eventBus is already injected at RunProfileHandler's constructor). The dry-run half adds a Skipped counter to DryRunProgressCounters and IEngineEventBus to DryRunStreamHandler's constructor.

Dry-run half: a DryRunStreamHandlerTests case whose fake engine bumps the shared counters' Skipped, asserting the warning is published AND that the frame sequence (chunks → progress → complete) is unchanged — that ordering is a wire contract. Update the two hand-constructions at DryRunStreamHandlerTests.cs:72 and :94.

roadmap.title: Give the three catalog-mutating handlers one answer to a failed reload
roadmap.rationale: SaveProfileHandler.cs:31-33 and DeleteProfileHandler.cs:25-27 log a warning and report success; RelocateProfilesHandler.cs:122-129 returns an ErrorResponse with a comment stating exactly why ('the catalog would keep serving the old directory's snapshot'). ProfileCatalog.Reload returns early on failure without swapping the snapshot or notifying subscribers, so on that path the service serves a stale catalog, broadcasts no ProfilesChangedEvent, and tells the client OK — while RunProfileHandler.cs:41 resolves the job's profile from that stale catalog.All, including a stale OnSuccessAction that may be PermanentDelete. Extract one CatalogReloadGuard and use it in all three. Reuse the existing PROFILE_SAVE_FAILED / PROFILE_DELETE_FAILED codes; keep relocate's existing message wording rather than forcing it into a shared template. The message must say plainly that the mutation DID reach disk but the list could not be refreshed.

roadmap.verification: tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/RelocateProfilesHandlerTests.cs pins the relocate branch and must stay green. Save and Delete have no dedicated tests — add two direct handler tests with an IProfileCatalog double whose Reload() fails, asserting ErrorResponse rather than ValidationResponse/OkResponse. Run EndToEndSmokeTests to confirm the happy path is unchanged. No UI change needed: IpcGateway.SaveProfileAsync/DeleteProfileAsync already surface IpcError.

roadmap.title: Warn when the profile catalog cannot be loaded at startup
roadmap.rationale: Completes the silent-success sweep. synthesis.notReported:
Patterns examined across src/, tests/ and benchmarks/ that came back clean, so their absence from the findings is informative rather than an oversight.

FROZEN FORMATS AND WIRE CONTRACTS — no violations found, and no finding in the roadmap requires one. Every serializable type reachable from Profile, IpcRequest/IpcResponse/EngineEvent, JournalRecord, DispositionAuditRecord, GlobalSettings, PersistedPauseState and UiState is listed in the correct JsonSerializerContext partial; the six contexts are correctly kept separate (internal on-disk shapes are not folded into the public FileManagerJsonContext). The order-as-contract sites are intact: JobPhase's declaration order still matches the progress publisher's backwards-sample drop, and VerificationMethod / RollbackAction / JobOutcome / SkipReason ordinals (int-serialized into the journal) show no reordering. The DryRunReport integer cross-references (SourceIndex/SubjectIndex/DirIndex/ParentIndex/RootDirIndex) are consistently emitted and assembled in one order. The hand-written *.snapshot writer and reader in DryRunSnapshotFormat still agree on all fourteen UTF-8 property literals. Two proposals that would have touched frozen surfaces were explicitly scoped out rather than accepted: the protocol 6→7 bump (deferred to a human decision) and any modification to GlobalSettings (the settings-rebase item works through SettingsService and the ...Serialized shadow properties instead).

AOT AND TRIM DISCIPLINE — clean. No assembly scanning, Activator.CreateInstance, Type.GetType, runtime proxies, config-binding frameworks or attribute-driven discovery of application types anywhere in shipping code. The only production reflection is EnumTitleExtensions.GetTitle reading [Tooltip] off enum field names, and it still carries the [DynamicallyAccessedMembers(PublicFields)] constraint that makes it trim-safe. The one behavior-changing DI proposal in the roadmap (GetServices<IIpcRequestHandler>) was checked against this rule specifically: it enumerates explicit registrations of concrete named types, which is not scanning.

LAYERING — no violations found. References point strictly downward (Contracts ← Core ← Platform.Windows ← hosts); the UI references Contracts only and never Core. The three sanctioned duplications have NOT drifted: EnginePaths.Default() / UiPaths / GlobalSettings.DefaultProfilesDirectory still agree on the same layout, and IpcEndpoint.Resolve() (client) still derives the same pipe name as WindowsIpcEndpointProvider (server). Core contains no OS-specific code beyond the single sanctioned OperatingSystem.IsWindows() probe in NormalizedPath. Two roadmap items were shaped by this constraint rather than fighting it — the save-blocking predicate is hoisted to Contracts (legal) rather than to Core (illegal, since the UI needs it), and IIpcConnection is defined in Contracts because its signatures are BCL-only.

WINDOWS INTEROP — clean. The [GeneratedComInterface] method declaration order for IFileOperation and IShellItem (which is the COM vtable layout, and where a reordering would silently call the wrong shell function and could delete the wrong file) is unmodified, as are the [LibraryImport] entry points and marshalling attributes in WindowsVolumeInfoProvider and WindowsPathCanonicalizer. No finding proposes touching any of it.

ON-DISK INFRASTRUCTURE MARKERS — clean. The .fm_staging / .pipeline_tmp / .fmtmp- names and the StagedPathFor layout are consistent between the writer, the scan exclusions and crash recovery's orphan discovery. The staged-replace consolidation in Tier 2 deliberately preserves the exact path shape; it changes only the guard, not the names.

FROZEN REGIONS — untouched and unassessed by design: third_party/TreeDataGrid (vendored submodule with local modifications), tests/FileManager.Scripts.Windows.Tests/**/profiles/*.json (the de-facto Profile compatibility corpus), the PowerShell environment builders, and BenchmarkDotNet.Artifacts/. Nothing in the roadmap edits any of them.

THE 17 IPC HANDLERS AS A SHAPE — deliberately not reported as duplication. Their similarity is the intentional replacement for reflection-based handler discovery under the AOT constraint. The findings against them are about the registration TABLES being hand-maintained and unguarded, never about the handlers themselves.

DELIBERATE NON-DEAD CODE — verified and left alone: DryRunSnapshotJsonContext (retained as the naive baseline the read-back benchmark measures against), SettingsService.MigrateLegacy and its two legacy string literals (the pre-v2 settings shim), and the [reserved — fails v1 validation] Profile members (SyncMode.Mirror in particular is live in the dry-run path). The four dead-code deletions in Tier 1 were each confirmed by repo-wide grep across .cs, .axaml, .json, .md and .ps1 — including the four x:CompileBindings=\"False\" regions, which bind by the same identifiers.

CONCURRENCY — no defect found. JobOrchestrator's tracked-task/linked-CTS pattern, ScanScheduler's claim/park/re-arm machinery (traced by hand: the two early returns in WorkerLoop exit outside the try's catch, so there is no double-decrement of _liveWorkers today), the DryRunRebuildGate supersede logic and the _applying re-entrancy guard all read correctly. Two items in the roadmap touch this area for OBSERVABILITY only, and one proposal that would have restructured shutdown ordering (IBackgroundWorkTracker) was explicitly rejected as speculative generality against an I-ATOMIC-JOB-governed sequence.

Not assessed at all: runtime performance (nothing was built, run or profiled — the benchmark suite is referenced as a gate, not as evidence), accessibility and visual design of the XAML, the docs/ tree except where cited as normative, and any behavior that only manifests against a real named pipe, a real registry, or a real filesystem under contention.

findings.title: The File.Replace → two-step-move fallback for staged overwrites is implemented twice, and the copies have already diverged
findings.claim: AtomicPlacer.ReplaceWithStaging/TwoStepReplace (Placement/AtomicPlacer.cs:343-372) and CrashRecovery.Replace (Journal/CrashRecovery.cs:470-485) implement the same operation — move temp into final while parking the prior version at staged, falling back to a two-step move when File.Replace is rejected — with the same three-exception filter (IOException, UnauthorizedAccessException, PlatformNotSupportedException) and the same log message. They have already drifted: AtomicPlacer's fallback guards with `if (File.Exists(finalPath))` and creates the staged directory, and its doc explains this idempotency is required so a retry cannot strand the final name absent; CrashRecovery's fallback does an unguarded `File.Move(final, staged); File.Move(temp, final);`.
findings.whyItMatters: This is the single most safety-critical write in the product: it is where a user's existing file is swapped for a new one while the prior version is preserved for rollback. Recovery re-runs the same journal rows on every startup, so a recovery pass that dies between CrashRecovery's two File.Move calls leaves the final name absent and the next pass throws FileNotFound on `File.Move(final, staged)` — exactly the stranded state AtomicPlacer's guard was written to prevent.

findings.title: RunProfileHandler launches an unowned background scan that no layer can observe, cancel, or drain at shutdown
findings.claim: A folder-scoped manual run fires `Task.Run(..., CancellationToken.None)` from inside the IPC handler. The resulting enumeration is owned by nothing: EngineHost's shutdown sequence drains only the orchestrator, so the scan keeps enqueuing into a queue whose consumer has stopped, and publishes its terminal RunQueuedEvent after the event bridge to IPC subscribers has been disposed.

evidence.excerpt: _ = Task.Run(() => ScanAndEnqueue(profile, typed.Path, runId), CancellationToken.None);

await _consumer.ConfigureAwait(false);                       // stop dequeuing
await Task.WhenAll(_running.Keys).ConfigureAwait(false);     // drain in-flight (I-ATOMIC-JOB)

// Always terminate the run, even on a fault or a zero-match scan: this event is the ONLY way
// a caller that got Scanning=true learns the outcome.

findings.whyItMatters: The handler's own comment says the RunQueuedEvent is the only way a client that received Scanning=true learns the outcome. If the user closes the app (which, in StartAndStopWithProgram mode, calls ShutdownServiceAsync) while a large folder scan is running, the enqueued payloads are dropped by a stopped consumer and the completion event fires into a disposed bridge — the UI shows neither "queued N files" nor an error, and the run silently never happened. The scan also holds ScanScheduler LongRunning worker threads that nothing waits on. No component in the composition root can see this work exists.
findings.proposedChange: Give the background enumeration an owner with a lifetime. Minimal version: inject `IHostApplicationLifetime`-equivalent cancellation into RunProfileHandler by adding a `CancellationToken` source the host controls — concretely, add a small `IBackgroundWorkTracker` to src/FileManager.Core/Observability/ with `void Track(Func<CancellationToken, Task> work)` and `Task DrainAsync()`, backed by a ConcurrentDictionary<Task,byte> and a linked CancellationTokenSource (mirror JobOrchestrator.cs:33/60-70, which already implements exactly this pattern). Register it in src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs beside the other Core singletons, inject it into RunProfileHandler in place of the bare `Task.Run` at line 85, and await `DrainAsync()` in EngineHost.RunAsync between `await orchestrator.StopAsync();` (EngineHost.cs:164) and `_eventBridge?.Dispose();` (line 167) so the terminal RunQueuedEvent still reaches subscribers. Pass the tracker's token into `scanner.Scan(profile, TriggerKind.ManualShell, folder, ct)` at RunProfileHandler.cs:103 so a shutdown cuts the walk short and the handler publishes RunQueuedEvent with the partial count plus an Error, which is already the shape ScanAndEnqueue produces on a fatal fault.

RunProfileHandler is constructed at 1 DI site (Program.cs:121) and 1 test site (EndToEndSmokeTests.cs:110) — both constructor signatures gain one parameter. tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/Handlers/Set3HandlersTests.cs also constructs it.

findings.verification: Add a Core test: start a folder run against a source tree, call DrainAsync concurrently, and assert exactly one RunQueuedEvent is observed on the bus and that no payload is enqueued after the drain returns. Existing coverage: tests/FileManager.Core.Tests/IPC/Handlers/Set3HandlersTests.cs already exercises RunProfileHandler's file and folder branches; those must stay green.
findings.verifierNote: The mechanism is real — RunProfileHandler.cs:85 fires `Task.Run(..., CancellationToken.None)` and calls scanner.Scan with no token, EngineHost.cs:164-168 drains only the orchestrator and then disposes the event bridge. But the harm is overstated, because TriggerQueue is a purely in-memory LinkedList (src/FileManager.Core/Watching/TriggerQueue.cs) with no persistence: EVERY pending payload is dropped at shutdown by design, so 'the scan keeps enqueuing into a stopped consumer' is not a defect specific to this call site. What is left is a shutdown-only edge case where a walk keeps burning scan-scheduler threads while the process is trying to exit, and one terminal event fires into a disposed bridge — at a moment when the UI that would consume it is closing. Downgraded to low, and the proposed remedy is oversized for it: a new IBackgroundWorkTracker abstraction in Core/Observability, a DI registration, and a change to the shutdown ordering (an area governed by I-ATOMIC-JOB) for a single call site is speculative generality. findings.title: The destination-sweep memory bound added for the streamed dry run was never applied to the batched dry run
findings.claim: DestinationProjector.Sweep takes a maxEntries budget that defaults to int.MaxValue. Space` and the final `Truncated` flag, so the engine emits sweep entries as ordinary chunks after the file-phase chunks; (b) move the survivor accumulation (`DestinationProjector.AccumulateSurvivors`, DryRunStreamHandler.cs:155), the sweep budget arithmetic (DryRunStreamHandler.cs:181), the `Task.Run` sweep hosting (lines 190-214), the `DryRunSpaceEstimator` folds (lines 84, 150-154, 225-227, 250-252) and the truncation reconciliation (lines 147, 216-222) into SimulateStreamAsync, beside the existing phase-3 block at DryRunEngine.cs:197-218; (c) remove `DestinationProjector destinationProjector`, `IVolumeInfoProvider volumes` and `EngineConfig config` from the DryRunStreamHandler constructor (DryRunStreamHandler.cs:26-28) and from src/FileManager.Service/Program.cs's implicit DI resolution; (d) leave in the handler ONLY the wire concerns: the `WireChunkConverter` (lines 271-304), the `DryRunProgressResponse` throttling loops, and the terminal `DryRunCompleteResponse`. rejected.title: IIpcStreamingRequestHandler inherits HandleAsync, so every streaming handler ships an unreachable throwing implementation of the sibling contract

Sixteen handlers honour the IIpcRequestHandler contract; the seventeenth throws NotSupportedException from it, and the test double does the same. The dispatch table is typed IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IIpcRequestHandler>, so the compiler presents a handler that cannot answer a request as if it can.

rejected.whyItMatters: The only thing keeping this safe is one ordering rule inside IpcServer.ServeConnectionAsync (the `is IIpcStreamingRequestHandler` test at line 185 must run before InvokeAsync at line 194). lensNotes:
**god-components**: METHOD. Churn was computed over the full history (`git log --format=%h --name-only --since="18 months ago"`), and the repo turns out to be one month old with 128 commits — so a file's commit count is a *share of all development*, not an aging signal. DryRunViewModel.cs at 42/128 (33%) and DryRunEngine.cs at 35/128 (27%) are not merely "hot", they are where essentially all recent work happened. I also computed pairwise co-change over the same window; the top ten pairs are all within the dry-run feature (DryRunViewModel.cs<->DryRunView.axaml 22, <->DryRunViewModelTests.cs 29, DryRunEngine.cs<->DryRunStreamHandler.cs 10, DryRunEngine.cs<->DryRunViewModel.cs 12 — the last being a cross-process, cross-assembly pair). Ranking therefore weighted the dry-run vertical heavily and everything else lightly; all five findings sit in it. That concentration is real, not a lens artifact.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED — large but stable (size alone is never a finding):
- ScanScheduler.cs (566 LOC, 4 nested classes, one `_lock` documented as guarding global thread accounting AND per-volume caps AND every session's parked-work stacks): 3 commits. The single-monitor design is arguably over-coupled, but nobody has needed to change it. Splitting a lock that is currently correct is pure risk with no observed cost.
- JobExecutor.cs (640 LOC, 12 constructor dependencies, 8 phases): 2 commits. CrashRecovery.cs (527 LOC, 6 responsibilities including re-implemented file primitives): 6 commits. AtomicPlacer.cs (402 LOC, 8 deps): 5 commits. These are the durable-safety substrate; they are long because they encode the spec's phase algorithm and I-RECOVER-FIRST ordering step by step, and per rule 7 that line-by-line correspondence to docs/specs/architecture-v1.md is a feature. Low churn confirms they are not where the pain is.
- ProfileValidator.cs (433 LOC, one Validate() fanning out to 10 check groups): 4 commits. This is the normative validation code table cross-referenced by the spec at §; a domain expert must be able to read the codes against the document. Rule 7 applies squarely. Not a finding.
- Job.cs (257 LOC, 20 public types, 10 commits): genuinely a grab-bag, and NormalizedPath — which defines the engine-wide lock order — is buried in a job-model file. I left it out because every one of those 20 types is frozen (JobOutcome/SkipReason ordinals are the on-disk journal's integer wire contract, and JobOutcome member NAMES are stringified into JobSummaryDto and switched on as string literals by ActivityViewModel.cs:98). Moving NormalizedPath to its own file is legal, but it is file organization with no measured cost, and the do-not-break register makes the surrounding types un-splittable. Not worth the risk budget.
- PathTruncation.cs / the Controls folder (602 LOC combined): 3 commits, and the pure rules are already extracted UI-free with tests. Correctly factored.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED — organization rather than responsibility:
- "DryRunViewModel.cs is 2751 lines / 20 top-level types, split the file." Raising this standalone would be a file-layout finding, which rule 6 excludes. The author already marked the six boundaries with banner comments (lines 22, 318, 1000, 1153, 2105, 2227), so the split is known and uncontested. I folded it into finding #1's proposedChange as a same-namespace file move, where it rides along with a change that has an actual cost attached.
- DryRunView.axaml (681 lines, 28 commits, 26% of all XAML). I checked whether the two tab markup blocks duplicate each other the way the view models do: after normalizing `Sources.`/`Destinations.` and the row type, the two ~140-line blocks differ by 86 lines — about half, not the ~85% the C# shows. That is real but much weaker, and the fix (a shared tab DataTemplate or UserControl) is best done as a follow-on once finding #1 lands and the two tabs share a base type. Not raised separately.
- SettingsViewModel.cs (575 LOC, 11 commits, 6 nominal responsibilities). I read it looking for the seam and did not find a compelling one. BuildCatalog is a declarative data block; ApplyFilter/BuildNavigation are small; the undo integration is delegated to UndoHistory; ChangeProfilesDirectory is one command with a callback seam and a try/finally. The parts are already separable by reading, and the tests are already split (SettingsViewModelTests, SettingsViewModelUndoTests, SettingsSearchTests). Per the brief's instruction: this one is closer to genuinely cohesive-despite-size than to a god class, and I am saying so rather than inventing a split.
- The 17 IIpcRequestHandler implementations. Explicitly excluded by the brief as the intentional AOT-safe replacement for reflection-based discovery. My finding #3 targets DryRunStreamHandler for carrying pipeline orchestration, which is a different complaint from their shape similarity, and it is careful not to disturb the RequestType key or the Program.cs dispatch list.

DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED — other lenses' territory:
- The batched dry-run path (DryRunRequest / DryRunHandler / IDryRunEngine.SimulateAsync / ReportBuilder / the byte-budget machinery) has no UI client: `grep -rn 'DryRunStreamRequest\|DryRunRequest' src/FileManager.UI/` returns exactly one line and it is the *stream* request.
